newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mortgage rates fell in week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mortgage rates fell in week.

text.p: Home mortgage rates fell this week as downbeat economic reports eased inflation fears and helped lower bond interest rates, Freddie Mac said Thursday.
Thirty-year fixed-rate mortgages averaged 7.85 percent in the week ending June 6, down from 7.94 percent last week, while 15-year mortgages dipped to 7.40 percent from 7.47 percent.
One-year adjustable mortgage rates fell to an average of 5.78 percent from 5.83 percent last week, Freddie Mac said.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 8.30 percent, the 15-year 7.80 percent and the adjustable loan 5.86 percent.

"The leading indicators were down one-tenth of a percent in April, and new home sales were also off 7.7 percent in April," said Frank Nothaft, Freddie Mac deputy chief economist. "This suggests some moderation of the very strong growth rate we saw in the first quarter of this year.
"Signs of a somewhat less-robust growth rate calmed inflation fears and that in turn helped interest rates ease up a little," Nothaft added.
On Friday the Labour Department will issue U.S. employment data for May.
Lenders charged an average of 1.7 percent in fees and points on 30- and 15-year loans, unchanged from last week. They charged 1.4 percent on adjustable loans, down from 1.5 percent the previous week.
Freddie Mac is a corporation chartered by Congress that buys mortgages from lenders and packages them into securities for investors.
